---
title: "Specific Heat near the Lambda Transition"
source_chapter: "10"
source_section: "10.6.4"
source_page: 292
---

> [!TLDR]
> The helium-4 lambda transition has a sharp but finite heat-capacity cusp because its critical exponent α is slightly negative.

Near a continuous transition, the singular part of the heat capacity follows a power law:

$$
{\thermal{C}}_{\mathrm{sing}}\sim A_\pm |t|^{-\alpha},\qquad t=\frac{{\thermal{T}}-{\thermal{T}}_c}{{\thermal{T}}_c}.
$$

The amplitudes above and below the transition can differ. The exponent determines the limiting behavior:

- $\alpha>0$: a power-law divergence.
- $\alpha=0$: a logarithmic divergence can occur, or a finite jump in a mean-field model.
- $\alpha<0$: the singular contribution tends to zero. A regular background can produce a finite cusp.

For the helium-4 lambda transition, the source gives $\alpha\approx-0.013$. Thus the heat capacity has a finite, very sharp cusp, rather than an infinite value.

**Fig. 10.4** Finite heat-capacity cusp at the helium-4 lambda transition. The illustrative curves use ${\thermal{C}}={\thermal{C}}_c-A_\pm|t|^{0.013}$ with a constant regular background and different amplitudes on the two sides. The axes have no absolute heat-capacity scale. The curve reaches the finite value ${\thermal{C}}_c$ at ${\thermal{T}}={\thermal{T}}_\lambda$. Its slope becomes singular.

> [!warning] Source correction — finite cusp
> The source sketch labels the peak as a divergence. For its stated helium-4 exponent $\alpha\approx-0.013$, the heat capacity stays finite. The new figure shows this finite cusp. A positive exponent would instead give a divergent heat capacity.

The amplitude ratio is universal within a universality class when the same definitions and limits are used. Individual amplitudes depend on the material. See [[10.07.03 Universality and Universality Classes]].

## Physical quantities

| Symbol | Unit | Quantity | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${\thermal{C}}$ | $\unit{J\,K^{-1}}$ | Heat capacity | Total heat capacity under the stated constraint. |
| ${\thermal{T}}$ | $\unit{K}$ | Temperature | Absolute temperature of the system. |
| ${\thermal{T}}_c$ | $\unit{K}$ | Critical temperature | Temperature of the stated phase transition. |
